For terrorism trauma in a prosecutor, 'Happy families' could plausibly trigger loss/safety themes, but 'Medical equipment such as needles or drips' points toward a medical trauma context that is not otherwise represented in the memory or appraisal items. This looks like a hard-to-explain trigger mismatch rather than ordinary heterogeneity.

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips
issues.explanation: 'I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened' is typically associated with interpersonal/sexual trauma or moral contamination themes. In this profile, the other appraisals are inaction guilt and distrust, and the memory items describe vivid, present-tense traumatic reliving of a terrorism event. Without any sexual assault, bodily violation, or contamination-related trigger/memory content, this appraisal is clinically discordant with the trauma type and the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips
issues.explanation: For a terrorism trauma in a 33-year-old prosecutor, the selected trigger set is weakly anchored to the trauma described. 'Needles/medical equipment' could occur if he sustained injuries, and 'alcohol smell' could occur if alcohol was present during aftermath or coping, but together they imply a medical/assault-like or hospital-associated cue pattern that is not supported anywhere else in the profile. With no memory or appraisal content linking the trauma to injury treatment, intoxication, or bodily violation, these triggers are clinically hard to place.

'I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened' is more typical of sexual assault, moral contamination, or exposure involving bodily fluids. In a terrorism case it is not impossible, but here it is not supported by the rest of the selected items: the memories emphasize disorganization and nowness, and the appraisals emphasize guilt and distrust, not bodily violation or pollution. This makes the contamination item the least coherent appraisal in the set.

issues.item: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: For an adult male prosecutor with terrorism trauma, the appraisal of feeling 'dirty or contaminated' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The other items center on sensory trauma triggers (alcohol smell, explosion sounds), disorganized yet vivid reliving memory, and guilt/distrust appraisals, which fit terrorism exposure. 'Contamination' more strongly suggests trauma involving sexual assault, bodily violation, or moral taint, and here it lacks support from the memory, trigger, or strategy nodes. This makes it a clinically questionable outlier within the allowed components.

vignette:
Ethan sat in the passenger seat of his wife’s car, the late autumn sun low and golden through the windshield, and felt the exhaustion wash over him like a tide he could no longer outrun. He was thirty-three years old, a prosecutor in a mid-sized city, married for six years, and for the past eighteen months he had been living with something he could not name. He had come to his first appointment because his wife, Rachel, had finally said she could not watch him disappear anymore. He had not argued. He was too tired.

The event that had shattered him had taken place on a weekday afternoon in October, two years ago. Ethan had been walking through the central plaza of the county courthouse complex, a public space he crossed every day, when a vehicle-mounted improvised explosive device detonated less than a hundred yards from where he stood. The blast threw him to the ground. He had no memory of the sound itself—only a pressure that seemed to come from inside his skull, and then the ringing, and the smoke, and the bodies. He had scrambled to his feet and moved toward the wreckage. He had pulled at debris. He had tried to help. But the man whose leg he had held while waiting for paramedics had died before they arrived. The woman who had been thrown against a concrete planter had been unconscious and bleeding from her ears. Ethan had stayed until the scene was cleared. He had gone home that night and told Rachel he was fine. He had not been fine.

What troubled him most, he said, was that he could not tell a clear story of what had happened, even to himself. The memory existed not as a narrative but as a series of sensory fragments that arrived without warning and without context. He would be standing in the shower, and suddenly he would be there again—the heat of the blast wave, the grit of pulverized glass on his tongue, the smell of alcohol from a broken bottle of hand sanitizer that had been on a security guard’s desk. That smell, specifically, had become a trigger. He could not walk past a bar without his chest tightening. He could not sit next to someone who had been drinking without feeling his pulse spike. He had stopped going to dinner with colleagues. He had stopped going anywhere.

The memories, when they came, were more real than normal. They had a vividness that ordinary recollections lacked, a kind of brutal clarity that made the present moment feel thin and false. He would be at his desk reviewing case files, and the memory of the blast would descend on him with such force that he would lose track of where he was. The past felt present. It was not remembering; it was reliving. And the worst part, the part that kept him awake at night, was the guilt. He could not forgive himself for not doing more. He had been a prosecutor. His job was to protect people. He should have seen the vulnerability of that plaza. He should have done something. He had failed.

This belief had grown roots. He had come to distrust others in a way he had not before. People smiled, they shook his hand, they said they understood, but he was certain that beneath the surface they were not what they seemed. He had stopped trusting his own judgment. He had stopped trusting anyone’s. At work, he had become withdrawn, delegating trials he would once have fought to lead. His supervisor had noticed. Rachel had noticed. He had noticed himself shrinking.

What finally brought him to seek help was not the nightmares, though they came most nights. It was not the way he flinched at the sound of a car backfiring or a door slamming, though he did. It was the exhaustion. The feeling of being tired all the time, bone-deep tired, as if he had been running for two years without stopping. He had come to believe that he would never feel safe again, and he was not sure he deserved to. But he was also afraid—afraid that if he let himself really think about what happened, he would not be able to put himself back together. He did not know if he wanted to be forgiven. He only knew he could not keep living this way.
